source.title: SAS: Simulated Attention Score
source.authors: Chuan-Yang Zheng; Jiankai Sun; Yi-Hang Gao; Yue-Hao Wang; Peihao Wang; Jing Xiong; Li-Liang Ren; Hao Cheng; Janardhan Kulkarni; Ye-Long Shen; Atlas Wang; Mac Schwager; Anderson Schneider; Xiao-Dong Liu; Jian-Feng Gao

record.file_problem: Whole paper text is present. There are minor formatting and transcription irregularities, but no material cutoff.
record.tranche_reason: The study reports language-model perplexity while varying model size and attention-head count, but it does not fit scaling laws or test extrapolation.
record.gate_note: Perplexity comparisons across model sizes bear on V1, and the head-count sweep bears on V4. The paper does not fit power laws, predict larger runs from smaller runs, or optimize parameter/token allocation under a fixed compute budget. Downstream benchmark scores are reported, but not as a prediction from scale or pretraining loss.
record.test_reason: Only the Section 3.1 head-count sweep bears on a version. It varies MHA heads (1 to 96) at a fixed hidden size of 768 (about 125M parameters, Arxiv, length 512) and reports validation perplexity, which is a shape-at-fixed-size test of V4. The rest of the paper compares the authors' SAS attention against baselines at a few sizes with fixed 50K steps. It fits no power laws and tests no extrapolation, compute-optimal allocation or downstream prediction from loss.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct: the authors conclude that head count and per-head hidden size are crucial to Transformer performance. They propose SAS to simulate more heads and wider features at moderate size, and report gains across lengths, datasets, sizes and downstream tasks.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates an attention architecture rather than fitting scaling laws, extrapolating from smaller runs, or finding compute-optimal parameter/token allocations.
record.method_sensitivity: Perplexity varies with attention-head count: the reported optimum is 12 heads, with gradual degradation at higher counts.

fits_no_version.finding: SAS, a modified attention that simulates more heads and wider per-head features at a small parameter overhead, lowers perplexity by about 2–5% vs MHA at matched nominal size (125M–10.6B).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Non-standard attention parameterisations at near-fixed parameter count can shift the loss curve, beyond standard shape variation.

record.problems: The study does not fit scaling curves or test extrapolation or compute-optimal allocation. Its model-size perplexity comparisons cover a limited set of sizes and settings; the head-count sweep does not report numeric values for most settings in the text.

untested.parts: No power-law fit. Sizes are compared only at a fixed 50K steps, three on Books3 and two on Pile, so data may be the bottleneck.
Depth, width and feed-forward ratio are not varied; only head count at fixed width, one model size, one dataset.
Downstream scores are reported per size and token count but not modelled as a function of scale or loss.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's limits_scope label on V4 rested on the authors' framing. The numbers show a roughly 4% perplexity spread across a 1–12 head range, consistent with V4's 'slight' effect. The degradation beyond 12 heads is shown only in Figure 1, without values. Kaplan et al. is cited only as a reference for MHA.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not fit or assess power-law shape or exponents, nor sweep parameters, tokens, and compute independently with the other factors non-bottlenecking.
The study varies attention-head count, but does not test depth or width over a broad range.

relationships.condition: MHA, about 125M parameters, hidden size 768, Arxiv, length 512, heads varied 1–96
relationships.reason: Perplexity spans only 6.08 (1 head) to 5.82 (12 heads), roughly 2.4% in loss, a small shape effect (r11, r15). The authors nonetheless call head count critical, and values beyond 12 heads are figure-only.
relationships.display_finding: Perplexity ranged from 6.08 with one head to 5.82 with twelve heads, corresponding to roughly a 2.4% difference in logarithmic loss.
